01 · Connect The Dots

Where Did The Claim Stop?

Connect the stages in order, then match the claim formats and evidence fields for both billing tracks.

From Intake To Adjudication

0:52
Read The Transcript

Transmit And MatchHere’s the part people miss. Start by matching the exact claim version to the payer acknowledgment. The billing system may show that the claim was sent, but that alone does not prove that the payer accepted it. If intake rejects the claim, identify the edit, route the correction, and verify acceptance of the replacement transmission.

Read The DecisionAn accepted claim can still be pending. Check whether the payer is waiting for anything and who owns the next step. Once adjudicated, match the remittance to the account and read the outcome at the claim or service line that actually changed.

Confirm ClosureA paid status is a starting point for reconciliation. Match the remittance and payment trace to the posted transaction. Close the financial work after the expected posting and any residual balance are explained.

Learn First

A Claim Moves Through Stages

The Concept

Coverage and documentation support the claim. After transmission, acceptance means it entered processing. Adjudication determines the outcome. Posting records that outcome on the account. Follow-up starts at the last stage you can prove.

Worked Example
  1. Find The StageThe clearinghouse shows “sent,” but the payer rejected a missing member ID at intake.
  2. Choose The Next StepBilling fixes the verified ID and confirms payer acceptance. There is no adjudicated denial to appeal yet.

Now Try It: Build the normal lifecycle first. Then ask where a rejected claim would loop back.

One Encounter Can Produce Two Claims
Hospital outpatient visitSame encounter · separate claim records
Professional servicePhysician EvaluationCMS-1500 · professional claim
Facility servicesHospital ResourcesUB-04 · facility claim
Learn First

One Encounter Can Have Two Claim Records

The Concept

A professional claim identifies the clinician’s service, setting and service line. An institutional claim identifies the facility’s bill, period and service categories. Each may have its own payer claim number, determination and payment.

Worked Example
  1. Clinician RecordFor a separately billed imaging interpretation, check the professional service line and rendering provider.
  2. Facility RecordFor the hospital’s imaging services, check the institutional bill type and revenue line. The clinician’s remit does not settle the hospital balance.

Now Try It: Match each format and field family to the record where you would look for it.

Form references: CMS Professional Billing · CMS Institutional Billing. The paper form names help identify each track; the 837 transactions are electronic.

02 · Drag And Arrange

What Needs Action First?

It’s . Rank these four accounts for today’s worklist. Use deadline risk, age, dollars and what is ready to work.

Choose What To Work First

0:41
Read The Transcript

Protect The DeadlineRead the queue for deadline risk before you rank accounts by dollars. A small denial with a receipt deadline tomorrow can come before a larger balance that is still inside a verified review window. Check the source of the deadline and what counts as received.

Weigh ActionabilityAsk what you can move today. An overdue claim with a verified owner or a ready packet is actionable. An account that is properly pending with nothing outstanding may need a dated check instead. Use age and dollars to compare accounts with similar urgency.

Leave A Work PlanWrite a short reason for the priority. Then name the next owner, the date, and the evidence that will show the action worked. That makes the queue decision usable by the next collector.

DeadlineAgeOpen ARActionability
Learn First

Prioritize What Can Be Lost Or Moved Today

The Concept

Start with documented deadlines and the action available now. Use balance, age and recoverability to break ties. An account still within confirmed turnaround can stay on a dated watch.

Worked Example
  1. Work FirstA $480 appeal is due tomorrow and the packet is ready. Send it to the designated queue and verify receipt.
  2. ScheduleA $9,000 claim is within confirmed review time with no near deadline. Assign a date to recheck its status.

Now Try It: Rank the new worklist and be ready to explain the evidence behind your top choice.

What To Record

“I worked [claim] first because [deadline] and [evidence ready]. For the pending claim, [owner] will check [status] on [date].”

Visual Reference · Two Billing Tracks

Read The Two Claim Forms

Identify the kind of bill and the fields that drive follow-up. These are first-page reference images from the Lab, not forms to complete.

One Visit, Two Claims

0:47
Read The Transcript

Professional ClaimAn outpatient hospital visit can produce a professional claim for the clinician and a separate institutional claim for the facility. On the professional claim, compare the rendering provider and place of service, then inspect the procedure, modifier, units, and diagnosis linkage when the denial points to those fields.

Institutional ClaimOn the institutional claim, start with the type of bill and statement period. Look at the relevant revenue line and compare the billed setting with the order and other supporting records. These fields answer different questions about the facility encounter.

Match Before ActingUse the claim identifiers and payer response for the specific bill you are working. A paid professional claim does not tell you whether the hospital claim was accepted, denied, or paid.

Compare The Fields And Codes

What Each Field Tells A Collector

QuestionPhysician · CMS-1500Hospital · UB-04
Where And How Was It Billed?POS describes the setting on a professional service line. For example, 11 is office and 22 is on-campus outpatient hospital. Compare POS with the documented setting when the payer flags a mismatch.Type of bill classifies the institution, bill type and frequency. For example, 0131 identifies a hospital outpatient original admit-through-discharge bill in the reference format. Verify the frequency and original claim reference before sending a replacement.
Which Service Or Department?CPT/HCPCS describes the service or item. Modifiers add context; for example, 26 identifies the professional component when the code and circumstances support it. Compare the exact code, modifier and units before attributing a denial to coding.Revenue codes identify facility service categories, such as 0762 for observation. A facility line can also carry a CPT/HCPCS code and units when applicable, such as G0378 for hourly observation. A revenue code is not a substitute for the procedure code.
What Diagnosis Supports The Bill?ICD-10-CM diagnoses describe the condition; a diagnosis pointer links a professional line to its listed diagnosis. Confirm the linkage against the record; do not change a diagnosis to obtain payment.The institutional bill reports diagnoses at claim level. The principal diagnosis and applicable present-on-admission information matter for inpatient review. ICD-10-PCS describes reportable inpatient hospital procedures; outpatient facility lines commonly use CPT/HCPCS when required. Do not use an outpatient rule to infer an inpatient code.
What Period And Provider Match?Check line dates, rendering and billing providers, and the service location. A clinician may bill professional work performed in a hospital; the professional claim still has a separate ID and remit.Check statement from/through dates, applicable admission and discharge details, patient status, and billing facility plus attending/operating provider where reported. Compare with the order, stay record and authorization.
What Affects Pricing?Compare the DOS fee schedule or contract to the exact line, modifier, setting and units. A contract may value facility and nonfacility settings differently.Verify the DOS contract and whether pricing uses a case rate, group, per diem or line basis. Medicare inpatient MS-DRGs and outpatient APCs are examples of payment groupings, not interchangeable diagnosis or revenue codes. Look for packaged services before summing expected payments.
Shared Fields Still Matter

Both tracks need the right patient, payer, claim version, dates, charges, provider identifiers and any applicable approval or prior-payer information. The way those details are reported differs. Use the matched claim and payer rules; leave coding changes to authorized staff.

Reference images only. Electronic claim layouts differ from paper forms. CMS Professional Guide · CMS Institutional Guide · CMS Payment Systems.

03 · Physician Billing

Investigate A Professional Claim

Open the claim image, encounter record and payer decision. Compare setting and line evidence before choosing the route.

Learn First

Compare The Exact Professional Service Line

The Concept

Read the submitted professional claim line beside the encounter record and payer decision. Check the setting, rendering provider, code, modifier and units relevant to the issue. Route verified claim data corrections through the authorized team.

Worked Example
  1. Find The MismatchA professional claim shows three units. Coding verifies the encounter supports two and approves that correction.
  2. Route And VerifyProfessional Billing follows the payer’s replacement instructions. AR checks acceptance of the linked claim and then its new determination.

Now Try It: Open all three records in the new case. Identify which field differs, what proves it and who can fix it.

Physician Review Lens

Match the rendering/billing provider, place of service, service date, code, modifier, units and diagnosis linkage where relevant. Route coding changes to authorized staff. The hospital’s facility claim does not answer a professional claim edit.

04 · Hospital Billing

Investigate A Facility Claim

Open the institutional bill, order and approval, and payer decision. Decide whether the bill needs a correction or the payer decision needs review.

Learn First

Compare The Facility Bill With The Order And Payer Match

The Concept

Read the bill type, statement dates and relevant revenue or service line. Compare them with the signed order and approval. Determine whether the provider submitted an error or the payer matched the wrong record.

Worked Example
  1. Find The MismatchA facility claim requests payment for an implant. The invoice receipt is tied to a different encounter number.
  2. Route And VerifyKeep the supported claim data. Use the payer’s approved records route to associate the invoice with the correct claim, then verify indexing.

Now Try It: Compare the institutional bill, order and decision. Choose the route supported by the evidence and the notice.

Hospital Review Lens

Check statement dates, type of bill, facility revenue lines and the documented setting. For an inpatient review, check admission/discharge details and grouping support where relevant. Outpatient observation does not become inpatient just because the encounter crosses midnight.

05 · Evidence Matching

A Denial Code Is A Clue

Match each symptom to the evidence you’d use to prove or rule out its cause. Then decide who can act.

From Payer Message To Verified Cause

0:44
Read The Transcript

Read The SymptomTreat a payer message as a lead. For example, no claim on file might mean the claim was rejected at intake, sent to the wrong payer, or searched with the wrong identifier. The message alone cannot tell you which happened.

Match The EvidenceCompare the internal transmission and payer acknowledgment for the same claim version. Then use the portal for a matched status or determination. If it cannot answer the open question and follow-up is due, use a verified payer contact to ask for the specific blocker or next step.

Choose The RouteRoute verified provider data errors to the right internal owner. Use the designated payer review route for a supported payer error. If a needed fact is still missing, document what you verified and assign a dated action to close that gap.

Learn First

The Reason Tells You What To Test

The Concept

A payer message is a clue. The root cause is what the matched claim, source records and payer evidence prove. If they disagree, record what is still unknown before choosing an action.

Worked Example
  1. Reported Reason“No claim on file.” The provider’s billing screen says it was sent.
  2. Proof To SeekMatch the transmission and payer acknowledgment to the same claim version. If the payer rejected it, correct the intake edit; if it was accepted, trace it with the payer.

Now Try It: Match each symptom to the evidence that would confirm or rule out its cause.

Reported ReasonWhat the payer said.
Verified CauseWhat the matched records show.
ResolutionWho can fix it, by when, and with what proof.
Document Studio · Two Samples

Read The Remit Before Moving The Balance

Trace each line from charge to adjustment, payer payment and patient share. Compare the remit with the claim and posting before deciding what to do.

Read A Remittance In Three Passes

0:49
Read The Transcript

Match The HeaderBefore reading the money, check that the payer, claim control number, service date, and relevant line match your account. A member explanation of benefits explains the decision. The provider remittance is where you review the provider's adjudication and adjustment details.

Follow The MoneyRead across the line. Separate the charge, payer payment, adjustment, and assigned patient share. Read the group code and adjustment reason together, plus any remark. An open balance by itself does not tell you what the patient owes.

Trace The PaymentFind the related payment trace and match it to the payment posted on the account. If an amount remains, determine whether it is supported patient share, an unresolved pricing variance, or another posting issue before you move the balance.

Training As Of These sample dates are generated from the day this course run started. They stay fixed when you resume.
1 · MatchCheck payer, claim version, service dates and provider.
2 · Read The LinesCompare amounts and group code, CARC and any RARC.
3 · ReconcileTrace payment, verify posting and choose the owner.
Learn First

Read The Remit In Three Passes

The Concept

Match the payer and claim first. Read the line amounts and the group code, adjustment reason and remark or notice. Last, match the payer payment to the trace and posted transactions before moving any balance.

Worked Example
  1. Follow The Dollars$200 billed and $140 allowed. The payer pays $120. The remit shows $60 contractual adjustment and $20 patient responsibility.
  2. Check The Outcome$200 = $120 paid + $60 adjustment + $20 patient share in this example. Verify the $120 posted and the $20 is still owed before collecting; the $60 is not patient responsibility.

Now Try It: Read both sample remittances. A denial with $0 paid does not by itself establish what the patient owes or the contract would allow.

EOB, ERA And EFT Are Different

A member EOB explains benefits and is not a bill. An electronic remittance advice (ERA) reports adjudication to the provider; a provider remittance may also be viewable on a portal. The EFT/check is the movement of money. Match the remit, payment trace and posted transactions; a claim payment amount need not equal a deposit covering many claims.

Code examples and display are instructional. For live accounts, verify the remit and plan policy. CMS Remittance Guidance · X12 CARCs · X12 RARCs.

06 · Two-Track Calculation

Find The Payment Difference

Calculate both examples. In these simplified cases, subtract validated patient share from the verified allowed amount, then compare with the actual payer payment.

Is It Underpaid Or Unreconciled?

0:49
Read The Transcript

Establish The Expected PayHere’s where the numbers get interesting. Use the rate that actually applies to the product, date, setting, and service. In a simple example with no other adjustments, an allowed amount of two hundred dollars minus a verified twenty dollar copay gives an expected payer payment of one hundred eighty dollars.

Compare With Actual PayIf the matched remittance and posting show a payer payment of one hundred fifty-five dollars, the supported difference is twenty-five dollars. Compare the bank trace with the posted transaction before calling it an underpayment so you can rule out a posting issue.

Separate Residual ARIf the account shows forty dollars open, investigate the remaining fifteen dollars separately. Keep the supported pricing variance, the total open balance, and any verified patient share distinct in your note.

Expected Allowed− Verified Patient Share= Expected Payer Payment− Actual Payer Payment= Variance
Learn First

Expected Payment Is Not The Same As Billed Charges Or Open AR

The Concept

Use the verified rate and covered units to find allowed. In these simplified cases, subtract validated patient share to find expected payer payment. Compare that with actual paid; investigate any remaining open balance separately.

Worked Example
  1. Physician · Line Rate2 units × $90 = $180 allowed. Less $20 patient share = $160 expected. Actual paid $140 → $20 variance.
  2. Hospital · Case Rate$5,000 case rate includes the related lines. No patient share. Actual paid $4,650 → $350 variance. Do not add packaged line charges to the case rate.

Now Try It: Calculate both new cases. Use each contract basis and show the expected amount before the variance.

Do Not Confuse Variance With The Open AR Balance

A posted balance can include another unresolved item. Verify contract basis, COB, applicable pricing rules and posting before deciding what to recover. Facility pricing may be case-based, grouped, packaged or otherwise contract-specific.

Appeal Workshop · H-407

Make A Supported Case For Review

Use the facility remit, order, authorization and prior review to build a realistic appeal. Practice routing and attaching evidence before recording an acknowledgment.

Build An Evidence-Based Appeal

0:51
Read The Transcript

Confirm Route And CutoffConfirm the designated submission route, who can submit, and when the packet must be received. A pending informal review does not give you more time unless the payer confirms an extension. Keep the deadline and the review turnaround separate.

Build The ArgumentIdentify the exact claim and determination you are disputing. State the discrepancy in a sentence, tie each supporting document to that issue, and request a specific outcome. For example, if the denial references the wrong setting, cite the bill, signed order, and matched approval.

Record The ReceiptOnce submitted, record the receipt date, tracking reference, and what was sent. Check indexing or determination at a dated checkpoint. After any favorable decision, verify the revised remit and posting before closing the financial work.

Fictional Payer Receipt Deadline: Use the deadline stated in this practice notice. Appeal rules and levels vary by payer and program.
Learn First

An Appeal Makes A Specific Case For Changing A Decision

The Concept

Use the payer notice to confirm the review level, destination and receipt deadline. Write the decision you dispute, the evidence that supports you and the outcome you request. Include only relevant records, then verify receipt and case indexing.

Worked Example
  1. IssueThe payer denied claim F-204 as a duplicate.
  2. EvidenceThe submitted claim and the cited original remit show different service dates. Attach both records and point out the difference.
  3. RequestAsk the payer to review the duplicate match and issue a revised determination. An acknowledgment proves receipt, not approval.

Now Try It: Use this structure for the facility authorization dispute. Check the formal route before drafting or attaching records.

The workshop is fictional and does not contact a payer. CMS First-Level Redetermination is one example of program-specific requirements.

07 · Account Notation

Leave A Note Someone Can Act On

Start with the payer’s determination, document your research, then finish with what you did and when to check the result.

Write A Note The Next Collector Can Use

0:52
Read The Transcript

Lead With The DeterminationPicture the next collector opening this account. Start with the payer determination. Name the E O B or remittance source, label the date as processed or remitted, and give the matched claim number and reason. If a separate denial date is available, include it. A pending claim may have no remittance or denial to cite.

Show What You CheckedThen write what you checked and what it proved. If you called, name the payer, the number dialed, who you spoke with, what they stated, and the call reference number. If you used the portal, identify the portal record and its reference.

Close With The Next CheckFinish with the action you actually completed, its receipt or task reference, and anything still planned. State the turnaround and what starts it if known. Give the next owner a date and the evidence they should verify.

Use This Notation Order

  1. EOB And Denial

    Per [payer] EOB in [source], dated [processed or remit date] ([date type]), claim [claim number / payer ICN] was denied on [denial date] due to [reason and code, if shown].

    Use the denial date only if the record shows it. If it does not, write “a separate denial date was not shown.” Do not infer a denial from a pending status.
  2. Checked And Verified

    Checked [internal records and external sources] and verified [specific findings].

    Include the claim version, documents or portal record that support the finding. Distinguish the payer’s reported reason from what you verified.
    Call Details · Only If A Call Occurred

    Called [payer name] at [phone number], SW [representative name]. Rep stated [what the representative confirmed or instructed]. Call Ref # [reference].

    SW means “spoke with.” For portal or chat research, name that source and its reference instead. Do not record a call that did not occur.

  3. Resolution And TAT

    Resolution: [action actually completed, date, channel or owner, items sent or changed, and receipt or task reference]. TAT: [turnaround, business or calendar days if stated, and what starts the clock]. Follow-up: [owner, date, and proof to check].

    If turnaround was not provided, say so and set a dated checkpoint to obtain it. A receipt confirms receipt; it does not prove payment or approval.
Read A Complete Note With A Payer Call
Learn First

Follow The Notation Sequence

The Concept

Open with the payer EOB and denial when there is one. Write what you checked, then any payer call. End with the action taken, the stated turnaround (TAT), and the follow-up owner and date.

Worked Example
  1. OpeningPer the payer EOB in Provider Exchange, dated Apr 3 (remit date), claim F-310 was denied for missing documentation. The EOB did not show a separate denial date.
  2. CheckedChecked the internal claim and portal notice; the notice requested the operative report.
  3. Resolution And TATSent HIM task FIC-20 to obtain the report. Nothing has been uploaded yet. TAT not provided; AR will check the task in two days.

Now Try It: Arrange the completed facility note. This case used the portal, so it does not need a call paragraph.

Learn First

Separate The Completed Action From The Payer Outcome

The Concept

Write the outcome the records actually support. Use the call format only if you spoke with a payer rep. Include the stated TAT and its starting point; a follow-up checkpoint is a separate date.

Worked Example
  1. Completed ActionSubmitted a verified correction and captured the transmission reference. Payer acceptance is still pending.
  2. TAT And Follow-UpPayer quoted 10 business days after acceptance. AR will check acceptance in two days; the payer clock has not started.

Now Try It: Use the supplied facts to assemble a note. Check the source, call reference if applicable, resolution, and TAT before you use it.

Notation practice is inspired by ARLearningOnline’s Scenario And Note-Preparation Approach. The cases and coaching here are original; actual payer and client rules take precedence.

Document Your Follow-Up On Claim P-218

You are the Professional AR collector. Review the Physician Claim File and write an account note for the next collector. Record the payer’s determination, the evidence you verified and the correction you would route to Billing.

Distinguish the planned correction from work already completed. No call or replacement submission occurred. Record the turnaround as unavailable and set a dated checkpoint for payer acceptance.

Learn First

Choose The Action That Addresses The Proven Problem

The Concept

Identify the last verified event, name who can move the claim, and choose a checkpoint that proves the action worked. Avoid routing by the balance or status label alone.

Worked Example
  1. Evidence To DecisionA payer requests a missing operative report. The correct report is available, and the notice names a records deadline. Send only the requested record to the designated queue.
  2. Decision To Follow-UpVerify receipt and association to the claim, then check adjudication. Receiving a file did not settle the balance.

Printable Reference

Insurance AR Desk Guide

Bring this checklist to either billing track. Use current payer instructions, contract terms and organizational policy in live work.

For Every Claim, Know The Purpose

ActionGoalEvidence To Leave
Rank the workProtect deadlines and work actionable risk.Age, dollars, urgency, documented rationale.
Verify the claimWork the right version and line.Payer/product, member, DOS, claim/ICN, line.
Trace historyFind the latest verified stage.Claim image, acknowledgment, remit, posted transactions, prior task/receipt.
Test the causeDistinguish a denial reason from the verified failure.Matched source, conflicting facts, proof still needed.
Reconcile moneySeparate pricing, posting and liability.Expected allowed/payment, actual, variance, open AR.
Route and actAssign the owner who can fix it and preserve rights.Action, route, deadline, evidence, receipt if sent.
Post the noteGive the next collector a usable handoff.EOB and denial → checked → call details if applicable → resolution, TAT and dated follow-up.
Verify outcomeConfirm a decision and reconcile posting before financial closure.Revised remit, deposit/trace, posting and residual disposition.

Action: Because [evidence] confirms [cause], [owner] will [action] via [route] by [date] so [result]. Follow-up: Check [proof] on [date]; escalate if [trigger].

Claim Statuses And The Next Question
Sent / Not On File
Which payer and version were sent? Find matched receipt before retransmitting.
Rejected
Which intake edit failed? Correct through the owner; obtain payer acceptance.
Accepted / Pending
What is still needed, and what is the verified turnaround? Set a date or escalate the overdue blocker.
Denied / Partially Paid
Which claim or lines, adjustment group, CARC and RARC? Verify whether this is a data error, payer decision, coverage issue or another cause.
Paid / Reversed
Does the current remit, EFT/check trace and posted transaction agree? Follow linked claim versions.
Coverage, Benefits And Approval

Verify eligibility on the date of service, the specific benefit and network, limits and dated accumulators when relevant. Check coordination of benefits (who pays first) and prior payer adjudication. Match approval to the exact code, dates, units, site, provider and setting. Active coverage or approval alone does not guarantee payment.

Resolution Options And Deadlines

Correct a verified claim-data error through Billing or authorized Coding. Request reprocessing for a supported payer error if that route is available. Use the designated appeal or payment-dispute route for a supported challenge. Route internal tasks with evidence and due dates; confirm payer escalation ownership and reference. Allow time only with verified status and a dated checkpoint. Transfer balances, issue patient communications, or request adjustments only when liability, policy and approvals support them.

Track original filing, replacement, records response, appeal and turnaround separately. Confirm the trigger, calendar or business days, and receipt rules. Informal review does not automatically extend a deadline. A packet receipt is not adjudication.

Use The Simulator After Practice

Rank the queue, submit your rationale and review the coaching key. Open the account and review balance, remit, transactions and prior notes. Choose portal or verified payer contact based on the question and case requirements. Validate the reimbursement and resolution, review the appeal workspace, and submit a simulated packet only when the case calls for it. Post your note and save the learner output as instructed.
